title: Anthropic's S-1, $518B in cloud commitments, and circular AI capex
content:
Anthropic's S-1, $518B in cloud commitments, and circular AI capex
While reading through Anthropic's Form S-1 SEC registration statement for its proposed Nasdaq IPO under ticker ANT today, a few infrastructure and accounting details in the footnotes stood out that show how much of Big Tech's AI revenue is the same pile of capital circulating between seven companies.
On October 26, 2026, Anthropic officially announced its S-1 filing with the SEC. Within minutes of the EDGAR upload (CIK 0002130357, Accession No. 0001628280-26-067168), developers and financial analysts started digging through the footnotes. What those footnotes reveal is not just the story of Claude. It is the blueprint for a $500B+ circular vendor-financing loop connecting Sundar Pichai (Google), Satya Nadella (Microsoft), Jensen Huang (NVIDIA), Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Elon Musk (xAI and Tesla), Tim Cook (Apple), Andy Jassy (AWS), and Dario Amodei (Anthropic).
Anthropic has filed an S-1 registration statement with the SEC related to its proposed IPO. Read more: anthropic.com/news/s1-sec Legal disclaimer: A registration statement relating to these securities has been filed with the SEC but has not yet become effective. These securities may not be sold nor may offers to buy be accepted prior to the time the registration statement becomes effective.

Inside Anthropic's Form S-1: $16.3B H1 Revenue, an $80.7B GAAP Loss, and $518B in Cloud Lock-In
Let's look at the raw numbers inside Anthropic's S-1 filing (anthropicpbc-sx1.htm) before we trace where the money goes. On the surface, Anthropic's top-line growth is the fastest enterprise software ramp in Silicon Valley history, driven by Claude Code and enterprise API adoption. Full-year revenue jumped 12x from roughly $381 million in FY 2024 to $4.6 billion in FY 2025. In the first six months of 2026 alone (H1 2026), revenue hit $16.286 billion, with Q2 2026 generating $11.555 billion in a single quarter.
Then you look down the income statement and contractual footnotes, and two massive realities jump off the page:
- The $80.748 Billion H1 2026 GAAP Net Loss: While Anthropic narrowed its H1 2026 core operating loss to $693 million and generated $3.929 billion in positive operating cash flow, its GAAP net loss for those six months was a jaw-dropping $80.748 billion. Why? Because $72.388 billion of that loss came from non-cash mark-to-market revaluations of convertible notes and derivative liabilities issued to hyperscaler backers like Amazon and Google as Anthropic's private valuation surged toward $965 billion.
- The $518 Billion Take-or-Pay Cloud Mortgage: As reported by The New York Times on Google's $40B Anthropic commitment, Google committed up to $40 billion ($10 billion immediate cash plus $30 billion milestone-contingent financing) on top of its earlier $3B+ stake, while Amazon expanded its $8 billion investment by up to another $25 billion (up to $33 billion total). In exchange, Anthropic signed non-cancellable multi-year cloud purchase commitments totaling $111.1B to $114.5B to Google Cloud through July 2033, $110B to AWS through April 2036, and $31.4B to $44.9B to Microsoft Azure through 2033. Including Broadcom TPU leases and GPU neoclouds, Anthropic is locked into roughly $450B to $518B+ of fixed infrastructure obligations over the next decade, with nearly 80% structured as rigid take-or-pay contracts.
- The 16% Cloud Marketplace Toll: In 2025, 47% of Anthropic's total revenue ($2.16 billion) flowed through AWS Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI marketplaces. For every dollar an enterprise spends on Claude through Bedrock or Vertex AI, Amazon and Google skim roughly 16 cents off the top in distribution fees before Anthropic pays those exact same clouds billions more to rent the underlying Trainium2 and TPU silicon.
Dario Amodei's Two Essays vs. The S-1 Balance Sheet: How Much Does a 'Country of Geniuses' Cost?
To understand why Anthropic signed $518 billion in non-cancellable cloud leases, you have to read Dario Amodei's two foundational essays side by side with the S-1 risk factors. In October 2024, Dario published Machines of Loving Grace: How AI Could Transform the World for the Better. In that essay, he coined the phrase "a country of geniuses in a datacenter": millions of autonomous frontier model instances smarter than Nobel Prize winners, running at 10x to 100x human speed, compressing 50 to 100 years of biological research, cancer cures, neuroscience, and economic development into a single 5 to 10 year window.
Fifteen months later, in January 2026, Dario published the darker companion essay, The Adolescence of Technology: Confronting and Overcoming the Risks of Powerful AI. Opening with Carl Sagan's famous question from Contact ("How did you survive this technological adolescence without destroying yourself?"), Dario mapped out five existential danger zones: autonomous alignment failures ("I'm sorry, Dave"), biological and cyber weaponization ("A surprising and terrible empowerment"), authoritarian surveillance ("The odious apparatus"), and in Section 4, titled "Player piano" after Kurt Vonnegut's novel, the risk of extreme economic disruption and wealth concentration in a tiny handful of compute-owning entities.
Here is the central paradox exposed by the S-1 filing: in The Adolescence of Technology, Dario warns that AI could concentrate unprecedented economic power in a few giant corporations. Yet nine months later, Anthropic's S-1 proves that surviving the compute race to build that "country of geniuses" required signing over $518 billion in take-or-pay infrastructure contracts to Google, Amazon, Microsoft, NVIDIA, and Broadcom. Even with Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust (Class T shares) and founder super-voting stock (Class F controlling 50.1%), a Public Benefit Corporation that owes half a trillion dollars in non-cancellable cloud rent cannot simply pause the treadmill when Wall Street expects quarterly growth.
Who Actually Runs on Whom? Deep Breakdown of the 7 AI Titans' Frenemy Stack
In public, Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Sundar Pichai, Satya Nadella, and Tim Cook position their companies as fierce rivals fighting for AI dominance. Under the hood, their infrastructure stacks are completely entangled. Every "competitor" is simultaneously a customer, supplier, landlord, or venture investor in the others:
Show Me the Code: Tracing a 'Multi-Model' Request Through the Frenemy Cloud Tollbooth
As Solutions Engineers and full-stack developers, we often design multi-provider model routers assuming we are diversifying our vendor risk across Anthropic, Meta, Google, and Apple. In reality, when you trace a production request in TypeScript, your API call hits the exact same three cloud balance sheets and two hardware bottlenecks. Just do not confuse multi-cloud routing with financial independence: both endpoints pay a ~16% marketplace toll to Anthropic's two biggest convertible-note holders, and every single TPU and Trainium2 chip underneath those endpoints is fabricated on TSMC 3nm CoWoS lines.
The Passive Index Funnel: How VOO, SPY, QQQ, VTI, FXAIX, and VT Put Every 401(k) in One AI Trade
You might think: "I don't buy private AI venture rounds or IPOs like ANT, I just dollar-cost average into low-cost index funds in my 401(k) and IRA." Because modern index funds are market-cap weighted, passive investing has turned into a giant momentum funnel. Every two weeks, automatic paycheck contributions from tens of millions of workers allocate 33% to nearly 50% of every retirement dollar

report.summary: Anthropic's S-1 reportedly reveals massive revenue growth, an $80.7B accounting loss, and $518B in take-or-pay cloud commitments, highlighting circular AI capex among Big Tech.
report.background: The article frames Anthropic's IPO filing as a window into the AI compute race. Model labs need enormous cloud capacity, while hyperscalers want strategic stakes and guaranteed demand. Anthropic reportedly filed an S-1 for a Nasdaq IPO under ticker ANT, showing fast enterprise adoption through Claude Code and APIs. But the filing also discloses large multi-year cloud purchase obligations to Google Cloud, AWS, and Azure, plus convertible notes and derivatives tied to hyperscaler backers. As private valuations surged, non-cash revaluations produced a huge GAAP loss. The broader context is a circular AI economy: Big Tech invests in AI labs, labs buy cloud and chips, and marketplace fees flow back to the same companies.
key_points: Revenue is growing at extraordinary speed but accounting losses are enormous. Anthropic reportedly hit $16.286B in H1 2026 revenue, with $3.929B positive operating cash flow and a narrowed $693M operating loss, yet posted an $80.748B GAAP net loss. About $72.388B came from non-cash mark-to-market revaluations of convertible notes and derivatives as valuation climbed.

The $518B cloud commitment is the filing's central risk. Anthropic reportedly locked into $111.1B-$114.5B with Google Cloud through 2033, $110B with AWS through 2036, and $31.4B-$44.9B with Azure through 2033, plus Broadcom TPU leases and GPU neoclouds. Nearly 80% is take-or-pay, meaning Anthropic must pay even if usage falls short.

Marketplace tolls make the circularity concrete. In 2025, 47% of Anthropic revenue reportedly flowed through AWS Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI. Those clouds take roughly a 16% distribution fee, then Anthropic pays them billions more for Trainium2 and TPU capacity. The same firms are investors, suppliers, landlords, and sales channels.

There is a strategic paradox. Dario Amodei's essays describe a compute-heavy "country of geniuses" and warn about extreme economic concentration. Yet the S-1 reportedly shows that pursuing that vision required half a trillion dollars in non-cancellable cloud rent, limiting Anthropic's ability to pause the treadmill even with public-benefit trust and founder super-voting structures.

Developers and passive investors share the exposure. Multi-cloud routing across Bedrock and Vertex AI improves uptime but not financial independence, because both endpoints feed the same cloud balance sheets and TSMC advanced packaging. Meanwhile, cap-weighted index funds in 401(k)s and IRAs funnel retirement savings into the same AI trade.

For developers, the filing is a reminder that model routing is not vendor-risk diversification. A router that fails over between Claude on Bedrock and Vertex AI may improve reliability, but both paths pay marketplace fees and depend on the same underlying silicon and cloud landlords. Teams should instrument token spend, cloud egress, marketplace markup, and concentration risk rather than assuming multi-cloud equals independence.

For the AI industry, vendor financing and take-or-pay contracts can make revenue look more circular and demand more locked-in. That may accelerate buildouts but also concentrate risk if growth slows. For regular users, pricing and product availability may depend on a few cloud providers' economics. For retirement savers, passive index funds may already provide broad exposure to the same AI capex cycle.

SEC EDGAR for the S-1 and footnotes; OpenCost or Kubecost for Kubernetes cost allocation; Infracost for infrastructure-as-code cost estimates; LiteLLM as an open-source multi-provider proxy with spend tracking; OpenTelemetry plus Grafana for request and cost telemetry. These help teams measure marketplace markup, token spend, and cloud concentration without treating multi-cloud routing as financial diversification.
